# Why Kōbe is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right
Some restorations are cosmetic. **Kōbe** is not — the marks in this name are the difference between reading the sources and guessing at them.

Kōbe is a city of thresholds: between mountain and sea, between ancient shrine and modern port, between Japan and the wider world. Its name comes from kanbe, the title of the families who served the Ikuta Shrine, and its modern identity was forged when it opened to foreign trade in 1868. The Nihon Shoki, Japan's second-oldest chronicle, records that Empress Jingū founded Ikuta Shrine in AD 201.  The shrine gave its name to the surrounding district and to the kanbe — shrine-supporting families — from whom the modern city of Kōbe takes its name.

That is the figure this file is about — and the temple now standing at its restored name.
## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Kōbe
- **ASCII form:** kobe
- **Meaning:** "Door to the gods or support door"
- **Domain of influence:** Port City, Hyōgo
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 神戸
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 131 of 271
## The Name Before the Marks

The name is attested as **神戸**. On the evidence, it means "Door to the gods or support door".

Strip **Kōbe** to *kobe* and one piece of evidence vanishes:

- **o → ō** — Macron: long vowel: the vowel length the ASCII form cannot show.

None of these marks is decoration. Each one is a fact about how the name was spoken, and each one is checkable against the scholarly record the temple cites.
## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Kōbe** lives at [/sites/kobe/](/sites/kobe/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/kobe/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/kobe/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/kobe/patterns/).

The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can say — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it in Tier-1: mechanically verifiable, information-rich.

Every flagship temple is hand-built to the same standard: the original script displayed with its provenance, the pronunciation reconstructed phoneme by phoneme, the sources named — because a restoration you cannot audit is just a spelling with confidence.
## The Archetype at Work

A temple is also a reading of what this figure *means* — and meanings have addresses in the modern world. The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) maps **Kōbe** to the industries its archetype genuinely resonates with, each match argued, weighted, and open to challenge:

- **Travel, Tourism & Place Branding** — Port city and beef; a global culinary destination.
- **Agriculture, Food & Harvest** — Kobe beef made the city a global food brand.
- **Maritime, Shipping & Ocean Industries** — A working port city; maritime trade is its founding economy.

This is the part of the file that surprises people: a four-thousand-year-old name, mapping cleanly onto twenty-first-century trades. The patterns are not marketing — they are the same myths, read forward.
## In the Sacred Texts

The Japanese tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Kojiki](/texts/kojiki/) and [Nihon Shoki](/texts/nihon-shoki/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on, free to read, cross-linked back to the names they mention. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
